1065.title: Empty minds, full bellies
1065.hook: don't prize the clever, and people won't compete (Tao Te Ching 3)
1065.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter three in different ways: some as advice to rulers, others as personal practice, noticing what they prize and letting go of contests that grow out of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was beauty and ugliness together: every name brings its opposite. Your line was without words, teaching by how the work is done.

On Monday the office starts a step challenge, with a leaderboard on the kitchen wall. By Wednesday people are pacing during phone calls. By Friday someone is walking laps of the parking lot at nine at night, and two old friends have stopped eating lunch together because one of them is, frankly, cheating. Nobody set out to make enemies. A board went up, and a contest grew out of it. Chapter three of the Tao Te Ching has a short, sharp idea about where contests come from.
screen: `A LEADERBOARD GOES UP.` → `LAPS AT NINE AT NIGHT.` → `WHERE DO CONTESTS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: First, what you prize, people chase. Legge's translation opens: "Not to value and employ men of superior ability is the way to keep the people from rivalry among themselves." Put a crown on cleverness, and everyone competes for the crown. The contest comes from the prize. Second, rare things make thieves. Don't treasure things that are hard to get, the chapter says, and people won't steal; don't parade what stirs up wanting, and minds stay settled. A rare sneaker, a hard-to-get ticket: the rarity is what makes people grab. Third, empty minds, full bellies. The sage, the chapter says, empties people's minds and fills their bellies, softens their ambitions and strengthens their bones. Readers hear this two ways. Some hear a ruler keeping people simple and quiet, and find it uneasy reading. Others hear a life not crowded with comparison: fed, sturdy, and not hungry for rank. The Chinese word here for mind also means heart, and some readers take the emptying as an emptying of wanting more than of thought. Readers still hold both views. Fourth, no contest. When the sage acts without forcing, the chapter closes, nothing falls out of order. Take the prize off the wall, and the race has nowhere to go.

segments.voice: Let your mind run over the last few days and find one scoreboard: who replied faster, who looks better, who works later. Picture taking that board off the wall, so the race stops and the other person is just a person again, and breathe there with nothing to win. If you pray, you can set the contest down in prayer; if not, let your shoulders drop as the race ends.
Empty minds. In chapter three, minds emptied of wanting and comparing, alongside full bellies and strong bones. Today's word.
Your line: no contest. With the prize off the wall, the other runner is just a neighbor again. Same time tomorrow.

1066.title: Empty, and never used up
1066.hook: the Tao is empty like a bowl yet never runs dry; it blunts sharp edges and unties knots (Tao Te Ching 4)
1066.howItsDone: Some Taoist meditation teachers use chapter four's lines about blunting sharp points and untying tangles as a reminder to soften and settle before sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was empty minds, emptied of wanting and comparing. Your line was no contest. Today the emptiness belongs to the Tao itself.

A necklace chain comes out of the drawer in one tight knot. The first move is to pull, and the knot gets smaller and harder, a little bead of metal you could never pick apart. The way out is the opposite of pulling. Lay it flat on the table. Loosen the middle with the tip of a pin. Give the loops room. Slowly the knot opens, not because anyone forced it, but because someone made space inside it. Chapter four of the Tao Te Ching is about that kind of space.
screen: `A CHAIN IN ONE TIGHT KNOT.` → `PULLING MAKES IT WORSE.` → `MAKE ROOM INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: First, empty like a bowl. The chapter compares the Tao to the emptiness of a vessel: you can use it and use it, and it never fills up and never runs dry. Strange arithmetic. Full things run out, and a full bowl can't take anything else. It's the empty part that does the work. Second, deep, and nobody's child. The chapter calls the Tao so deep it seems like the ancestor of everything. Then it ends with a shrug that's almost funny: it doesn't know whose child the Tao is. It only says the Tao seems to come before even the Lord on High. Third, blunt the sharp, untie the knot. In Legge's words: "We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of things." Sharp points: the cutting remark, the edge in a voice. Complications: tangles like the chain. The same lines come back in chapter fifty-six, as if the old master wanted them heard twice. Fourth, soften the glare. Soften your brightness, the chapter goes on, and settle in with the dust of everyone else. Not shining at people, not standing above the tangle, but getting down next to it, the way you'd lay a chain flat and give it room.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one tangle in your life right now, a misunderstanding, a messy email thread, a decision you've been tugging at for weeks, and for now, just stop pulling on it. Breathe into the middle of it and ask which one small loop could loosen first, the way a pin loosens a chain. If you pray, you can bring the knot into prayer; if not, keep breathing space into it.

Your line: untie the knot. Space does what pulling never could. See you at chapter five.

1067.title: Straw dogs
1067.hook: heaven and earth aren't sentimental; they treat things like straw dogs used in a ritual (Tao Te Ching 5)
1067.howItsDone: Readers of chapter five sometimes use the straw dogs as a reminder that misfortune isn't aimed at them, letting events be what they are before deciding how to respond.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was empty: the Tao like a bowl, used and never used up. Your line was untie the knot.

Does the rain know it's your wedding day? Months of planning. The chairs are out on the lawn, flowers tied to the ends of the rows, and at ten in the morning the sky opens. It's very hard not to take it personally. Why today? Why us? But the same rain falls on the farmer who prayed for it, on the parking lot, on the stray cat under the porch. It isn't aimed. Chapter five of the Tao Te Ching says something blunt about this, with a strange object: a dog made of straw.
screen: `RAIN ON THE WEDDING.` → `WHY TODAY? WHY US?` → `IT ISN'T AIMED.`

segments.voice: First, heaven and earth aren't sentimental. They don't act out of a wish to be kind, the chapter says; in Legge's words, "they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with." And the sage treats people the same way. That can sound cold. Hold on to it a moment. Second, what a straw dog was. Another old Chinese book, the Zhuangzi, home of the river god who met the sea on day one thousand thirteen, describes them. Before the ritual, straw dogs were kept in fine boxes, wrapped in embroidered cloth, handled with care by people who had fasted. After the offering, they were thrown out, walked over in the road, swept up by grass-gatherers to burn. Honored, then discarded. Not out of spite. The ritual was simply over. Third, a bellows. The space between heaven and earth, the chapter goes on, is like a bellows: empty, yet never used up, and the more it moves, the more comes out. The world isn't keeping score of anyone. It just keeps breathing. And a quiet warning: lots of talk wears out fast; better to keep to the center. Fourth, a neighbor with another spirit. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus says God "sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." There, rain on everyone is a sign of the Father's goodness, and a reason to love even enemies. In chapter five, the same impartial rain shows that heaven isn't sentimental. Two traditions, two meanings, the same weather.

segments.voice: Think of something recent that wasn't aimed at you: a delayed flight, a cold that came the week of a trip, a price that went up. Notice the why-me story your mind has wrapped around it, and set the story down beside the event, so you're looking at the event alone. If you pray, you can hold it in prayer just as it is; if not, breathe out and let it be weather.
Straw dogs. Ritual figures, honored and then thrown away when the rite was over; chapter five says heaven and earth deal with all things like that. Today's word.
Your line: not personal. The same rain fell on the farmer and the stray cat. Chapter five, done.

1068.title: The valley spirit
1068.hook: the valley spirit never dies; it is the mysterious female (Tao Te Ching 6)
1068.howItsDone: Some Taoist practitioners connect chapter six with gentle breathing practice, following an old commentary that reads the gate of the mysterious female as the nose and mouth; other readers take it as a picture of the world's source.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was straw dogs, honored and then discarded: heaven and earth aren't sentimental. Your line was not personal.

Hikers climb the peak for the view, take the photograph, and head back down. Nobody stays up there. The farms are below, in the valley: the river, the deep soil, the orchards, smoke from kitchen chimneys. The high place is admired. The low place is where things grow. Chapter six of the Tao Te Ching is barely a few lines long, and it chooses the valley as its picture of something that never dies.
screen: `THE PEAK GETS THE VIEW.` → `THE VALLEY GETS THE FARMS.` → `THE LOW PLACE IS WHERE THINGS GROW.`

segments.voice: First, the valley never dies. Legge put this chapter into rhyming verse, and it begins: "The valley spirit dies not, aye the same." A valley is a hollow, defined by what isn't there. Because it's low and open, it keeps receiving rain, snowmelt and rivers, and it doesn't wear out. Second, the mysterious female. The chapter names the valley spirit the mysterious female, the dark mother. The book reaches for a picture of birth: the Tao not as a ruler giving orders from above, but as a mother from whom everything comes, low and hidden and endlessly giving. Third, its gate is the root. The gate of this mysterious female, the chapter says, is the root of heaven and earth. That's the third gate in a week: the border gate, the gate of the mystery in chapter one, and now this, each an opening, not a wall. One old commentary, traditionally credited to a figure called Heshang Gong, reads the chapter in the body: the valley nourishing the spirit, and the gate as the nose and mouth, where breath comes and goes. Other readers keep it as a picture of the world. Fourth, used gently. This power goes on unbroken, the chapter ends, used gently, without strain. The valley never forces anything. It stays low and open, and the water arrives.

segments.voice: Get low if you can: sit on the floor, lie down, or lean back and let something take your weight. Breathe gently through the nose and notice the breath arriving on its own, the way water arrives in a valley without being called. If you pray, you can pray from this low place; if not, simply rest there.
The valley spirit. Chapter six's picture of what never dies: low, open, receiving, the mysterious female whose gate is the root of heaven and earth. Today's word.

1069.title: Last, and first
1069.hook: heaven and earth last because they don't live for themselves; the sage puts himself last (Tao Te Ching 7)
1069.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter seven into small daily choices, stepping back in lines, conversations and traffic, as a way of not living only for themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the valley spirit: low, open, and never dying. Your line was the valley.

A four-way stop, late afternoon. Two cars arrive at the same moment. One driver waves: go ahead. The other waves back: no, you. A little dance of hands through windshields, then somebody goes, and both drivers are smiling as they pull away. Nobody lost anything but a few seconds. And for a moment, two strangers who'll never meet were on the same side. Chapter seven of the Tao Te Ching is about the strange strength of going last, and it starts with the sky and the ground.
screen: `TWO CARS, ONE MOMENT.` → `GO AHEAD. NO, YOU.` → `NOBODY LOST ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: First, heaven and earth last. Legge's translation opens: "Heaven is long-enduring and earth continues long." Why? Because, the chapter answers, they don't live for themselves. The sky doesn't hoard its rain; the ground doesn't keep its harvest. They give everything away, and they go on and on. Second, the sage puts himself last. In Legge's words, "the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place." He treats his own self as if it were outside him, and yet his self is kept safe. Not grasping, and somehow not lost. Third, not a trick for getting ahead. The chapter ends with a question: isn't it because the sage has no private aims that his aims are fulfilled? Readers take this two ways. Some hear a strategy: hold back, and you'll end up ahead. Others say that going last in order to be first misses it, because the point was not to live for yourself at all. The chapter doesn't settle it. Fourth, an echo in Matthew. At the end of a parable where workers hired at the last hour are paid first, the King James reads: "So the last shall be first, and the first last." The parable keeps its own meaning, and the chapter keeps its own. What they share is an upside-down order.

segments.voice: Picture the places today where there'll be a small line: a doorway, a coffee counter, a merge onto the highway, a turn to talk in a meeting. See yourself stepping back at one of them with a small gesture, go ahead, and notice what it costs, which is probably very little. If you pray, you can offer that small step back; if not, just rehearse the gesture.

Your line: last, and first. Two strangers waving each other on are, for a moment, on the same side. Rest well.

1070.title: Like water
1070.hook: the highest good is like water: it benefits all and seeks the low places (Tao Te Ching 8)
1070.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching keep chapter eight's opening words, the highest good is like water, written where they will see them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was last: heaven and earth endure because they don't live for themselves. Your line was last, and first.

A glass tips over at dinner. In a second the water is everywhere it can reach. It runs along the grain of the table, slips under the edge of a plate, finds the one low spot by the salt shaker, and drips off the corner. Nobody told it where to go. It didn't argue with the plate. It went around. Water seems to know exactly where the lowest place is. Chapter eight of the Tao Te Ching looks at that and sees the highest good.
screen: `A GLASS TIPS OVER.` → `IT WENT AROUND.` → `IT FINDS THE LOWEST PLACE.`

segments.voice: First, it benefits all things. The highest good, the chapter opens, is like water. In Legge's translation: "The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things." It waters the rose and the weed without sorting them first. Second, it takes the place nobody wants. Water settles without striving in the low places people dislike, and that, the chapter says, is why it's close to the Tao. The valley, the one who goes last, the empty bowl: water is all of them at once. Third, good ground, deep heart, right timing. Then comes a short list that's easy to skip. In a home, goodness like water is the ground it stands on. In the heart, depth. In giving, kindness. In speech, being trustworthy. In leading, good order. In work, ability. In action, good timing. Ordinary virtues, the kind that show up in a kitchen or an office on a weekday. Water isn't only humble. It's useful, steady and on time. Fourth, it doesn't quarrel. The chapter ends on its plainest line: because water doesn't contend, no one finds fault with it. It goes around the plate, and gets where it was going anyway.

segments.voice: If you can, pour a little water slowly into a sink, a bowl or a plant, and watch where it goes: it doesn't push; it spreads, finds the low point and settles. Then sit with your eyes on it, or on the memory of it, and let each breath settle low in your body the same way. If you pray, you can pray with the water in front of you; if not, just keep watching.
Like water. Chapter eight's picture of the highest good: it benefits all things, takes the low place nobody wants, and doesn't quarrel. Today's word.
Your line: like water. It goes around the plate, and it keeps on going. That's chapter eight.

1071.title: Stop before it spills
1071.hook: better to stop than to fill a cup to the brim; retire when the work is done (Tao Te Ching 9)
1071.howItsDone: Some readers use chapter nine as a check on overwork and excess, choosing to stop a task when it is done well enough rather than polishing or adding past that point.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was like water: it benefits all things and doesn't quarrel. Water fills things; today asks how full is too full.

A mug of coffee, poured right to the rim, carried from the counter to the couch. Every step is a negotiation: eyes locked on the surface, tiny shuffling steps. A little slops over anyway, onto the hand, onto the rug, and the whole walk is spent guarding the cup instead of enjoying it. One more splash from the pot did all that. Leave a finger's width at the top and the walk is easy. Chapter nine of the Tao Te Ching opens with a full vessel of its own, then gives three more pictures like it.
screen: `POURED RIGHT TO THE RIM.` → `GUARDING THE CUP.` → `ONE MORE SPLASH.`

segments.voice: First, the cup. Legge's translation begins: "It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full." Not empty; just not full to the brim. The last bit of filling is what makes the carrying hard. Second, the blade. Keep sharpening an edge, the chapter says, and it won't keep its sharpness for long; past a point, more work only wears it away. Third, the hall of treasure. Fill a hall with gold and jade, and no one can guard it all; when wealth and honor make someone proud, they bring harm on themselves. A cup, a blade, a treasure hall, a proud name: each something good, pushed one step too far. The chapter isn't against coffee, or sharp knives, or wealth. It's about the extra splash. Fourth, the way of heaven. The chapter's last line, in Legge's words: "When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven." Seasons do this. Summer doesn't stay on to be admired; it does its work and steps back, and autumn comes. Stopping, here, isn't failure or quitting. It's knowing when the work is done.
screen: `THE CUP: NOT TO THE BRIM.` · `THE BLADE: SHARPENED AWAY.` · `THE HALL: TOO MUCH TO GUARD.` · `THE WORK DONE, STEP BACK.` · then, large: `STOP BEFORE IT SPILLS.`

segments.voice: Look over today and tomorrow for the place you're about to pour one more splash: one more email tonight, one more episode, one more edit to something already finished. Picture yourself stopping a little short of the rim, and notice what it's like to carry the cup with room at the top. If you pray, you can ask for help stopping; if not, breathe with the room you've left.
Stop before it spills. Chapter nine's cup, blade, treasure hall and proud name, and its last line: when the work is done, step back. Today's word.
Your line: stop before it spills. A week of chapters ends here: no contest, untie the knot, not personal, the valley, last and first, like water, and now this. I'll be here tomorrow.
